lessons.title: Implicit first and second derivatives
lessons.summary: Differentiate the whole relation before inserting a point.
lessons.objective: Find first and second derivatives on a specified smooth implicit branch.
lessons.before: Review the chain and product rules, tangent gradients and implicit first derivatives from A Level Pure Mathematics. A branch means one local choice of y as a function of x.
lessons.ideas:
Every occurrence of y depends on x

Differentiate both sides of the defining relation. For example, differentiating a product xy gives y+xy′. Differentiating a power of y requires its chain factor y′. Do not insert the coordinates before differentiating: that would turn the relation into a numerical equality and destroy its derivative information.

\[\begin{gathered}F(x,y)=0\\F_x+F_y y^{\prime}=0\\y^{\prime}=-\frac{F_x}{F_y}\qquad(F_y\ne0)\end{gathered}\]

The subscript notation is a compact summary: Fₓ means differentiating F with y temporarily fixed. In routine work you may differentiate the original equation directly. The condition Fᵧ≠0 ensures this local formula gives a finite gradient.

Differentiate again with the product rule

\[\begin{gathered}F_{xx}+2F_{xy}y^{\prime}\\\quad+F_{yy}(y^{\prime})^2+F_y y^{\prime\prime}=0\end{gathered}\]

The two mixed terms have different product-rule origins and combine to give the factor 2. When only values at a point are needed, first calculate y′ there, then insert x, y and that derivative into the twice-differentiated equation. This is often shorter than finding a large general formula for y′′.

When the relation already contains a derivative

If p=y′ appears in an equation, differentiate p as p′=y′′. Such a relation is not an ordinary curve F(x,y)=0, so do not apply the preceding partial-derivative shortcut while ignoring its p-variable. Keep the original branch and logarithm restrictions throughout.
lessons.method:
1. Check the point lies on the original curve and record its domain.
  2. Differentiate the relation, retaining every chain factor.
  3. Find the first derivative at the required point.
  4. Differentiate again before substituting numerical values.
  5. Check any denominator used to define the local branch.
mistakes: Differentiate y² as 2yy′, not 2y.
Both factors of xy contribute a derivative.
Differentiate products involving y′ again.
Substitute the point after differentiating.
A zero branch denominator requires separate analysis.

examples.title: 1 · A product term contributes twice
examples.question: Find y′ and y′′ at (1,2) on \(x^2+xy+y^2=7\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}2x+y+(x+2y)y^{\prime}=0\\y^{\prime}=-\frac45\\2+2y^{\prime}+2(y^{\prime})^2+(x+2y)y^{\prime\prime}=0\\y^{\prime\prime}=-\frac{42}{125}\end{gathered}\]

At the point, x+2y=5≠0. Insert the first derivative into the second equation; the squared derivative is positive even though y′ is negative.

examples.title: 2 · Differentiate a derivative product
examples.question: Find y′ and y′′ at (1,1) on \(y^3+xy=2\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}(3y^2+x)y^{\prime}+y=0\\y^{\prime}=-\frac14\\(3y^2+x)y^{\prime\prime}+6y(y^{\prime})^2+2y^{\prime}=0\\y^{\prime\prime}=\frac1{32}\end{gathered}\]

The product (3\(y^{2}\)+x)y′ contributes a derivative of its coefficient and a derivative of y′. Differentiating the remaining y supplies the second y′ term.

examples.title: 3 · A logarithm and its original domain
examples.question: On the branch xy>0, find y′ and y′′ at (1,1) on \(\ln(xy)+y^2=1\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac1x+\frac{y^{\prime}}y+2yy^{\prime}=0\\y^{\prime}=-\frac13\\-\frac1{x^2}+\left(2-\frac1{y^2}\right)(y^{\prime})^2\\\quad+\left(2y+\frac1y\right)y^{\prime\prime}=0\\y^{\prime\prime}=\frac8{27}\end{gathered}\]

Use the derivative of ln(xy) directly on its domain. The calculation does not require extending ln x+ln y to branches where the individual logarithms are not real.

examples.title: 4 · The equation already contains p
examples.question: A twice-differentiable function satisfies \(p^3+2x^2+y^2=14\), where p=y′ and y(1)=2. Find y′(1) and y′′(1).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}p(1)^3=14-2-4=8,\qquad p(1)=2\\3p^2p^{\prime}+4x+2yp=0\\12p^{\prime}(1)+4+8=0\\y^{\prime\prime}(1)=-1\end{gathered}\]

The real cube has one real root. Differentiating \(p^{3}\) gives 3\(p^{2}\)p′, and p′ is the requested second derivative.

lessons.title: Parametric gradients and concavity
lessons.summary: Differentiate with respect to x through the parameter.
lessons.objective: Calculate both derivatives, including the extra division by dx/dt.
lessons.before: Complete the preceding lesson. Review the chain, product and quotient rules and use exact values.
lessons.ideas:
Two coordinate functions, one curve

\[\begin{gathered}x=X(t),\qquad y=Y(t)\\\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{Y^{\prime}(t)}{X^{\prime}(t)}\\\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac1{X^{\prime}(t)}\frac d{dt}\left(\frac{Y^{\prime}}{X^{\prime}}\right)\end{gathered}\]

Both formulae require X′(t)≠0. The second derivative is the rate of change of the gradient with x, not with t. Replacing it by Y′′/X′′ is incorrect.

Useful combined form

\[\begin{gathered}\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{X^{\prime}Y^{\prime\prime}-Y^{\prime}X^{\prime\prime}}{(X^{\prime})^3}\end{gathered}\]

This follows by differentiating the quotient and dividing once more by X′. It is useful for exact substitution, but retain the original domain of t before cancelling factors.

Tangent exceptions

At a regular horizontal tangent, Y′=0 and X′≠0. If X′=0 while Y′≠0, the tangent is vertical and a finite dy/dx does not exist. If both vanish, these shortcuts decide neither tangent direction nor regularity; investigate the local behaviour separately. A second-derivative sign change only describes an inflection when it occurs along a suitable regular branch.
lessons.method:
1. Differentiate X and Y with respect to t.
  2. Divide Y′ by X′ and retain excluded parameter values.
  3. Differentiate this quotient with respect to t.
  4. Divide by X′ once more.
  5. Find coordinates from the original parametrisation, not from derivative ratios.
mistakes: Do not use Y′′/X′′ for the second derivative.
The extra division by X′ changes the sign in some domains.
Retain parameters cancelled from a ratio.
Check X′≠0 at a claimed horizontal tangent.
Give coordinates as well as parameter values when asked.

examples.title: 1 · The second division matters
examples.question: For \(x=t^2+2\), \(y=t^3-t\), t>0, find both derivatives in terms of t.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}X^{\prime}=2t,\qquad Y^{\prime}=3t^2-1\\\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3t^2-1}{2t}\\\frac d{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=\frac32+\frac1{2t^2}\\\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{3t^2+1}{4t^3}\end{gathered}\]

The restriction t>0 makes X′ positive and non-zero. The last expression is positive throughout this branch.

examples.title: 2 · A reciprocal parameter with a restriction
examples.question: For \(x=t+t^{-1}\), \(y=t-t^{-1}\), t>1, find the gradient and second derivative at t=2.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{t^2+1}{t^2-1}\\\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\frac{4t^3}{(t^2-1)^3}\\\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{t=2}=\frac53\\\left.\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right|_{t=2}=-\frac{32}{27}\end{gathered}\]

The excluded value t=1 makes X′ vanish. Do not fill that missing derivative by cancellation.

examples.title: 3 · A trigonometric parametrisation
examples.question: For \(x=3\sin t\), \(y=2\cos t\), 0<t<π/2, find both derivatives and evaluate the second at t=π/6.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac23\tan t\\\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\frac2{9\cos^3t}\\\left.\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right|_{t=\pi/6}=-\frac{16\sqrt3}{81}\end{gathered}\]

The cosine is positive on this parameter interval, so the curve is concave down throughout it.

examples.title: 4 · Horizontal and vertical tangents differ
examples.question: For \(x=t^2\), \(y=t^3-3t\), find all horizontal tangents and examine the tangent at t=0.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}Y^{\prime}=3t^2-3=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t=\pm1\\t=-1:\ (x,y)=(1,2)\\t=1:\ (x,y)=(1,-2)\\t=0:\ X^{\prime}=0,\quad Y^{\prime}=-3\ne0\end{gathered}\]

At t=±1, X′=±2 is non-zero, so both are regular horizontal tangents. At (0,0) the tangent is vertical: x=0. This point is not another stationary point of y as a differentiable function of x.

lessons.title: Hyperbolic and inverse-function derivatives
lessons.summary: Derive the rules and respect the principal real branches.
lessons.objective: Differentiate compositions using justified inverse-function signs and domains.
lessons.before:
Complete the preceding lesson. Review the chain, product and quotient rules and use exact values.

Review Hyperbolic functions, including principal inverses and logarithmic domains.
lessons.ideas:
Start from exponentials

Differentiating the exponential definitions gives the first two rules below; the quotient rule gives the third. Derivatives of the reciprocal functions then follow from differentiating a reciprocal.

\[\begin{gathered}(\sinh x)^{\prime}=\cosh x,\quad(\cosh x)^{\prime}=\sinh x\\(\tanh x)^{\prime}=\operatorname{sech}^2x\\(\operatorname{sech}x)^{\prime}=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x\\(\operatorname{cosech}x)^{\prime}=-\operatorname{cosech}x\operatorname{coth}x\\(\operatorname{coth}x)^{\prime}=-\operatorname{cosech}^2x\end{gathered}\]

Use the chain rule for every non-trivial argument. Cosech and coth exclude zero from their domains.

Undo the function, then choose the right sign

For y=asinh x, differentiate sinh y=x. Cosh y is positive, so it becomes √(1+\(x^{2}\)). For y=acosh x, the principal branch has y≥0; a finite derivative requires x>1. For inverse tanh, use its real open domain.

\[\begin{gathered}(\sinh^{-1}x)^{\prime}=\frac1{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\\(\cosh^{-1}x)^{\prime}=\frac1{\sqrt{x^2-1}}\quad(x>1)\\(\tanh^{-1}x)^{\prime}=\frac1{1-x^2}\quad(|x|<1)\end{gathered}\]

Inverse means a function that undoes the original map, not its reciprocal.

\[\begin{gathered}(\sin^{-1}x)^{\prime}=\frac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}},\quad|x|<1\\(\cos^{-1}x)^{\prime}=-\frac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}},\quad|x|<1\\(\tan^{-1}x)^{\prime}=\frac1{1+x^2}\end{gathered}\]

The minus sign for inverse cosine follows because sin y≥0 on its principal interval. A composition can create a corner even when its expression is defined: a principal square root can introduce |x|, which must be analysed from both sides.
lessons.method:
1. State the real domain and principal branch.
  2. Derive or select the appropriate base derivative.
  3. Multiply by the derivative of the inner function.
  4. Differentiate again with all product and chain factors.
  5. Check endpoints and both sides of any absolute value.
mistakes: Inverse hyperbolic functions are not reciprocals.
Acosh is defined at 1 but its ordinary derivative there is not finite.
Asin endpoints belong to its domain but not to its finite-derivative interval.
Do not replace √(x²) by x without a sign restriction.
A chain factor is needed for 2x just as for a more complicated argument.

examples.title: 1 · Combine product and chain rules
examples.question: Find f′ and f′′ for \(f(x)=\cosh(2x)\sinh x\), and give both derivatives at zero.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}f^{\prime}=2\sinh(2x)\sinh x\\\quad+\cosh(2x)\cosh x\\f^{\prime\prime}=5\cosh(2x)\sinh x\\\quad+4\sinh(2x)\cosh x\\f^{\prime}(0)=1,\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(0)=0\end{gathered}\]

The inner argument 2x supplies a factor 2. Both terms of the first derivative must be differentiated again.

examples.title: 2 · An inverse-sinh composition
examples.question:
Find both derivatives of

\[\begin{gathered}y=\sinh^{-1}(3x+1)\end{gathered}\]
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}y^{\prime}=\frac3{\sqrt{1+(3x+1)^2}}\\y^{\prime\prime}=-\frac{9(3x+1)}{[1+(3x+1)^2]^{3/2}}\end{gathered}\]

The radicand is positive for every real x. In the second derivative, the outside exponent −1/2 and the inside derivative 6(3x+1) combine with the original factor 3.

examples.title: 3 · Domain before differentiating
examples.question: Find the domain and both derivatives of \(y=\tanh^{-1}(2x-1)\).
examples.solution: \[\begin{gathered}-1<2x-1<1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0The derivative formula is used only inside the original open interval. Its algebraic expression outside that interval does not extend the real inverse-tanh function.

examples.title: 4 · A principal inverse produces a corner
examples.question: For \(f(x)=\cosh^{-1}(1+2x^2)\), decide whether f is differentiable at zero.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}f(x)=2\sinh^{-1}|x|\\f^{\prime}(0^-)=-2,\qquad f^{\prime}(0^+)=2\end{gathered}\]

The identity follows by taking cosh of the non-negative quantity 2asinh|x|. The one-sided derivatives differ, so the function is continuous but has a corner at zero. A two-sided derivative-based Maclaurin expansion at zero is unavailable.

lessons.title: Stationary points and local geometry
lessons.summary: Find every regular candidate and justify its nature.
lessons.objective: Classify horizontal tangents, inflections and parameter boundary cases.
lessons.before: Complete the preceding lesson. Review the chain, product and quotient rules and use exact values.
lessons.ideas:
Find all candidates in the actual domain

For a smooth explicit function, solve y′=0. For F(x,y)=0 at a regular point, solve F=0 together with Fₓ=0, then check Fᵧ≠0. For a parametrisation solve Y′=0 while checking X′≠0. The denominator is part of the regularity test, not a factor to discard without comment.

Nature needs evidence

A positive second derivative at a stationary point gives a local minimum; a negative one gives a local maximum. If the second derivative vanishes, this test is inconclusive. Check the gradient or concavity on both sides. A stationary inflection has a horizontal tangent and a change of concavity, without a local extremum.

Local versus global

A local second-derivative test alone does not prove a global bound. To prove a global minimum, establish a gradient sign change on the whole domain, strict convexity with an attained critical point, or a completed square with the correct substituted range.

Parameters and missing endpoints

The open range of tanh is (−1,1). A stationary equation tanh x=k has a solution exactly for |k|<1; at k=±1 it has no finite solution. Classify the equality cases separately. Tangent and normal equations also need separate treatment at zero or infinite gradient.
lessons.method:
1. Solve the complete stationary conditions in the stated domain.
  2. Check regularity and all denominator restrictions.
  3. Use the second derivative when it is non-zero.
  4. If it is zero, check signs on both sides.
  5. Give every coordinate and justify any global claim separately.
mistakes: A zero second derivative does not prove an inflection.
A vertical tangent is not a stationary point of a smooth y(x).
Keep every branch satisfying the stated domain.
An asymptotic parameter endpoint may not produce a finite stationary point.
A local extremum is not automatically a global extremum.

examples.title: 1 · Both stationary branches of an ellipse
examples.question: Find all stationary points of \((x-y)^2+4y^2=16\), classify them and give tangent and normal at the upper point.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}F_x=2(x-y)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y\\(x,y)=(2,2),\ (-2,-2)\\y^{\prime\prime}=-\frac1{4y}\quad\text{at these points}\\(2,2):\ y^{\prime\prime}=-\frac18\\(-2,-2):\ y^{\prime\prime}=\frac18\end{gathered}\]

The upper point is a local maximum, with tangent y=2 and normal x=2. The lower is a local minimum. The branch denominators are non-zero at both points.

examples.title: 2 · A unique global minimum
examples.question: Find the minimum of \(g(x)=\ln(\cosh x)-\frac{x}{2}\) on the real line.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}g^{\prime}=\tanh x-\frac12,\qquad g^{\prime\prime}=\operatorname{sech}^2x>0\\x=\frac12\ln3\\g_{\min}=\ln2-\frac34\ln3\end{gathered}\]

Tanh increases through 1/2 exactly once. The gradient is negative before and positive after, proving a unique global minimum. The positive second derivative independently confirms its local nature.

examples.title: 3 · A stationary point without an extremum
examples.question: Classify the origin on \(f(x)=\sinh^{-1}x-x\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}f^{\prime}=\frac1{\sqrt{1+x^2}}-1\\f^{\prime\prime}=-\frac{x}{(1+x^2)^{3/2}}\end{gathered}\]

The first derivative is negative except at zero, so there is no gradient sign change. The second derivative is positive to the left and negative to the right. Thus (0,0) is a stationary point of inflection, with tangent y=0.

examples.title: 4 · Two parameter values, two points
examples.question: Find and classify all stationary points for \(x=t^2+1\), \(y=t^3-6t\), t real. Also locate the vertical tangent.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}Y^{\prime}=3t^2-6=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t=\pm\sqrt2\\t=-\sqrt2:\ (3,4\sqrt2),\quad y^{\prime\prime}=-\frac{3\sqrt2}{4}\\t=\sqrt2:\ (3,-4\sqrt2),\quad y^{\prime\prime}=\frac{3\sqrt2}{4}\end{gathered}\]

The upper point is a local maximum and the lower a local minimum. At t=0, X′=0 but Y′=−6≠0, giving a vertical tangent x=1 through (1,0), not an additional stationary point.

lessons.title: Maclaurin polynomials and approximations
lessons.summary: Connect derivatives, coefficients and justified local estimates.
lessons.objective: Find the requested first few terms and distinguish coefficients from derivatives.
lessons.before: Complete the preceding lesson. Review the chain, product and quotient rules and use exact values.
lessons.ideas:
Match derivatives at zero

\[\begin{gathered}f(x)=f(0)+f^{\prime}(0)x\\\quad+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2!}x^2+\frac{f^{(3)}(0)}{3!}x^3+\cdots\end{gathered}\]

The coefficient of \(x^{n}\) is f⁽ⁿ⁾(0)/n!, not f⁽ⁿ⁾(0). To recover the derivative from a coefficient, multiply by the factorial. Here the aim is the first few terms requested, not a general formula for all n.

Differentiate, compose or use a local relation

Compute only as many derivatives as needed. For compositions, keep enough terms in each inner expansion: a leading \(x^{2}\) may mean that only two terms of the outside series are needed through \(x^{4}\). On an implicit branch, verify the point and branch condition before finding the derivatives. If the question asks for derivation by differentiation, show those derivatives even when a known series could check the result.

State what the truncation means

Write the requested polynomial and an appropriate remainder order. Big-O records the order of omitted terms near zero; it does not by itself provide a numerical error bound at every x. An asymptotic approximation is an estimate, not an exact equality. The expansion must refer to a real, sufficiently smooth branch in a neighbourhood of zero.

Extract the leading behaviour

For a limit, cancel the terms explicitly and identify the first surviving power. Even or odd symmetry can explain missing powers. A corner such as a leading |x| term prevents the ordinary two-sided derivative-based expansion at zero.
lessons.method:
1. Check the function has the required smooth real branch near zero.
  2. Calculate the derivatives or permitted subsidiary series.
  3. Divide each derivative by the correct factorial.
  4. Retain every term up to the requested degree or number of non-zero terms.
  5. Label estimates and justify any claimed error bound.
mistakes: A coefficient is not the corresponding derivative.
The first three non-zero terms need not have degrees 0,1,2.
Do not truncate the inner series too early.
An approximation is not an exact value.
A function defined at zero need not be differentiable there.

examples.title: 1 · A whole cubic polynomial
examples.question: Find the Maclaurin polynomial through \(x^{3}\) for \(f(x)=\frac{e^{2x}}{1+x}\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}f(0)=1,\quad f^{\prime}(0)=1\\f^{\prime\prime}(0)=2,\quad f^{(3)}(0)=2\\f(x)=1+x+x^2+\frac{x^3}{3}+O(x^4)\end{gathered}\]

Divide the second and third derivatives by 2! and 3!. Multiplying the exponential and reciprocal series gives the same coefficients, providing a separate check.

examples.title: 2 · A fourth derivative from an even series
examples.question: Find \(\ln(\cosh2x)\) through \(x^{4}\), and deduce its fourth derivative at zero.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\cosh2x=1+2x^2+\frac23x^4+O(x^6)\\\ln(\cosh2x)=2x^2-\frac43x^4+O(x^6)\\f^{(4)}(0)=4!\left(-\frac43\right)=-32\end{gathered}\]

The logarithm contributes both its first-order term and minus half the square of that term. Even symmetry rules out odd powers.

examples.title: 3 · Build the local implicit branch
examples.question: The branch through (0,0) satisfies \((1+x)y+y^2=x\). Find its polynomial through \(x^{3}\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}y=ax+bx^2+cx^3+O(x^4)\\a=1,\quad b+a+a^2=0\\c+b+2ab=0\\y=x-2x^2+6x^3+O(x^4)\end{gathered}\]

Equating successive coefficients gives a=1, b=−2 and c=6. The defining expression has derivative 1 with respect to y at the origin, so this is the unique smooth local branch through that point.

examples.title: 4 · A leading term determines a limit
examples.question: Find the first two non-zero terms of \(\sinh^{-1}(2x)-2x\) and hence its ratio to \(x^{3}\) as x→0.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}f^{(3)}(0)=-8,\qquad f^{(5)}(0)=288\\\sinh^{-1}(2x)-2x=-\frac43x^3+\frac{12}{5}x^5+O(x^7)\\\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sinh^{-1}(2x)-2x}{x^3}=-\frac43\end{gathered}\]

The linear terms cancel. Divide the remaining expansion by \(x^{3}\); the higher powers then tend to zero. The odd symmetry explains the missing even powers.

lessons.title: Mixed problems and later-topic links
lessons.summary: Combine derivative methods while keeping prerequisites explicit.
lessons.objective: Apply chain-rule substitutions and local series without losing domains or initial data.
lessons.before:
Complete the preceding lesson. Review the chain, product and quotient rules and use exact values.

The seven differential-equation extensions (Q2, Q13, Q26, Q34, Q39, Q44 and Q62) require linear first- and second-order differential-equation methods from later FP2 study. Q60, Q65 and Q77 require integration and, where supplied, the arc-length formula. Attempt those after learning the stated methods; the other four written problems consolidate this chapter.
lessons.ideas:
Differentiate a substitution explicitly

For w=φ(y), write both w′=φ′(y)y′ and w′′=φ′′(y)(y′)²+φ′(y)y′′. This explains how a nonlinear combination may become linear in w. Transform initial data too, including the first derivative.

\[\begin{gathered}w=\phi(y)\\w^{\prime\prime}=\phi^{\prime\prime}(y)(y^{\prime})^2+\phi^{\prime}(y)y^{\prime\prime}\end{gathered}\]

Changing the independent variable

If u=u(x), apply the chain rule twice. The second derivative contains two terms, because du/dx also depends on x.

\[\begin{gathered}y_x=y_u u_x\\y_{xx}=y_{uu}(u_x)^2+y_u u_{xx}\end{gathered}\]

Keep restrictions required for a reversible substitution, such as x>0 for u=ln x, or a positive branch when recovering a square root. Check the recovered solution in the original relation and against all initial data.

Approximations used in integrals

A short local series can produce an approximate integral. Integrate the complete polynomial, state the integration interval, and label the result as approximate. A rigorous bound needs a separate argument controlling the remainder over the whole interval. These applications do not replace learning the later integration chapter.

One method can check another

Implicit differentiation can supply Maclaurin coefficients; an eliminated parametric equation can check both derivatives. Keep the domain obtained from the original parametrisation. A correct algebraic formula without that domain is not a complete description of the curve.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the core skill and any later-topic prerequisites.
  2. Write first and second chain-rule relations before substitution.
  3. Transform domains and initial data together.
  4. Solve only with justified later methods, then recover the original variable.
  5. Check the original equation and label truncated-series estimates.
mistakes: The second derivative of a composition has two chain-rule terms.
Initial derivatives also change under substitution.
Recover the specified real branch, not both square roots automatically.
A truncated integral is approximate.
An eliminated equation must retain the parametrisation’s domain.

examples.title: 1 · A dependent-variable substitution
examples.question: Near x=0, \(y^{\prime\prime}+(y^{\prime})^2+2y^{\prime}=4e^{-y}\), y(0)=ln2 and y′(0)=1/2. Use w=\(e^{y}\) to recover y.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}w^{\prime\prime}+2w^{\prime}=4\\w(0)=2,\qquad w^{\prime}(0)=1\\w=2x+\frac32+\frac12e^{-2x}\\y=\ln\left(2x+\frac32+\frac12e^{-2x}\right)\end{gathered}\]

Multiplying the original equation by \(e^{y}\) gives the transformed equation. Solving it uses later linear-ODE methods. The logarithm is real on a neighbourhood of zero because its argument equals 2 there. Substitution verifies both initial conditions.

examples.title: 2 · Change the independent variable twice
examples.question: For x>0, solve \(x^2y^{\prime\prime}+xy^{\prime}-4y=0\) with y(1)=3 and y′(1)=2, using u=ln x.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}xy_x=y_u,\qquad x^2y_{xx}=y_{uu}-y_u\\y_{uu}-4y=0\\y=Ax^2+Bx^{-2}\\A+B=3,\qquad2A-2B=2\\y=2x^2+x^{-2}\end{gathered}\]

The x y′ term cancels the negative yᵤ term arising from the second derivative. Later constant-coefficient ODE methods give the two independent exponential solutions in u.

examples.title: 3 · A labelled integral estimate
examples.question: Use the series through \(x^{4}\) for \(\ln(1+x^2)\) to estimate its integral from 0 to 1/5.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\ln(1+x^2)=x^2-\frac{x^4}{2}+O(x^6)\\\int_0^{1/5}\ln(1+x^2)\,dx\\\quad\approx\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^5}{10}\right]_0^{1/5}=\frac{247}{93750}\end{gathered}\]

This is an estimate, not an exact antiderivative evaluation. On this interval the next term of the alternating logarithm series bounds the pointwise error by \(x^6/3\), so the integral error is at most \(\frac{(1/5)^7}{21}\).

examples.title: 4 · A local branch supplies a tangent and a series
examples.question: The branch through (0,0) satisfies \(y+xy^2=x+x^2\). Find y′(0), y′′(0), its tangent and its cubic Maclaurin polynomial.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}y^{\prime}+y^2+2xyy^{\prime}=1+2x\\y^{\prime}(0)=1,\qquad y^{\prime\prime}(0)=2\\y=x+x^2-x^3+O(x^4)\\\text{tangent: }y=x\end{gathered}\]

The derivative with respect to y of the defining expression is 1 at the origin, so there is a smooth local branch. Substituting its proposed cubic into the original relation cancels all coefficients through degree 3.

questions.title: The whole implicit gradient
questions.prompt_html: On a regular local branch of \(x^{2} + x y + y^{2} - 10=0\), find the complete expression for y′ as a rational function in x and y. Use numerator; denominator.
questions.solution_html: Differentiate all three terms: 2x+B y+(B x+2y)y′=0. The displayed rational function applies only where its denominator is non-zero.

questions.title: An implicit inverse-trigonometric derivative
questions.prompt_html:
A curve is defined by

\[- 3 x + \sin{\left(2 y \right)}=0,\qquad -\frac13\lt x\lt \frac13,\quad -\frac\pi4\lt y\lt \frac\pi4.\]

Write \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\).

  1. Use implicit differentiation to prove that

    \[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2 p^{2} \tan{\left(2 y \right)}.\]
    [3]

  2. Hence find the exact second derivative at \((\frac{1}{6},\frac{\pi}{12})\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(q=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\). Implicit differentiation gives

\[2 p \cos{\left(2 y \right)} - 3=0.\]

Differentiate once more:

\[- 4 p^{2} \sin{\left(2 y \right)} + 2 q \cos{\left(2 y \right)}=0.\]

Since \(\cos2y\ne0\) on the stated branch, divide by \(2\cos2y\) and rearrange:

\[q=2 p^{2} \tan{\left(2 y \right)}.\]

(b)

The first differentiated relation gives \(p=\sqrt{3}\). Substituting into the identity gives

\[q=2 \sqrt{3}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate twice before using the original relation.

(b)

Evaluate the first derivative as well as the trigonometric factor.

questions.title: Transforming a nonlinear equation through sine
questions.prompt_html:
A smooth function satisfies, on a neighbourhood of \(x=0\),

\[y^{\prime\prime}-\tan y\,(y^{\prime})^2+4y^{\prime}+4\tan y=e^{-x}\sec y,\]
\[y(0)=\frac\pi6,\qquad y^{\prime}(0)=\frac1{\sqrt3},\qquad -\frac\pi2\lt y\lt \frac\pi2.\]

  1. Put \(w=\sin y\). Show that \(w^{\prime\prime}+4w^{\prime}+4w=e^{-x}\).

    [4]

  2. Find the local solution for \(y\) that satisfies the initial data.

    [8]

  3. Find \(y^{\prime\prime}(0)\) without differentiating the inverse sine twice.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The chain and product rules give

\[w^{\prime}=\cos y\,y^{\prime},\qquad w^{\prime\prime}=\cos y\,y^{\prime\prime}-\sin y\,(y^{\prime})^2.\]

Multiply the original equation by \(\cos y\), which is non-zero on the stated branch. Substitute these expressions to obtain the required linear equation.

(b)

The auxiliary equation is \((m+2)^2=0\), giving \(w_c=(A+Bx)e^{-2x}\). For a particular integral \(Ce^{-x}\), substitution gives \(C=1\). Thus

\[w=(A+Bx)e^{-2x}+e^{-x}.\]

The initial values become \(w(0)=1/2\) and \(w^{\prime}(0)=\cos(\pi/6)/\sqrt3=1/2\). Hence \(A+1=1/2\) and \(B-2A-1=1/2\), giving \(A=-1/2,B=1/2\). On the given branch,

\[y=\sin^{-1}\!\left(e^{-x}+\frac{x-1}{2}e^{-2x}\right).\]

This is the local branch through \(\pi/6\); it is used only while the inverse-sine argument stays in \((-1,1)\).

(c)

The transformed equation gives \(w^{\prime\prime}(0)=1-4(1/2)-4(1/2)=-3\). At zero the chain-rule relation gives \(-3=(\sqrt3/2)y^{\prime\prime}(0)-1/6\). Hence \(y^{\prime\prime}(0)=-17/(3\sqrt3)\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate sin y twice, then multiply the original equation by cos y.

(b)

Translate both initial conditions to w, including the cosine factor in w′.

(c)

Use the already derived expression for w″.

marking_criteria.description_html: Multiply the original equation by cos y.
Try and determine the exponential particular integral.
Return to y with the inverse sine.
Use w″=cos y y″−sin y(y′)² at zero.

questions.title: A hyperbolic product with a global bound
questions.prompt_html:
\[f(x)=\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\qquad x\in\mathbb R.\]

  1. Show that \(f^{\prime}(x)=\operatorname{sech}x(1-2\tanh^2x)\).

    [3]

  2. Find all stationary points and determine their nature.

    [5]

  3. Prove directly that \(|f(x)|\le1/2\) for every real \(x\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The product rule gives

\[f^{\prime}=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh^2x+\operatorname{sech}x\operatorname{sech}^2x.\]

Use \(\operatorname{sech}^2x=1-\tanh^2x\) to obtain the required form.

(b)

Since \(\operatorname{sech}x\gt 0\), a stationary point requires \(\tanh^2x=1/2\). Thus \(x=\pm\ln(1+\sqrt2)\). At these points \(\operatorname{sech}x=1/\sqrt2\), so the values of \(f\) are \(\pm1/2\). Differentiating the factored first derivative and setting \(1-2\tanh^2x=0\) gives \(f^{\prime\prime}=-4\operatorname{sech}^3x\tanh x\). It equals \(-1\) at the positive point and \(1\) at the negative point.

(c)

Put \(v=\tanh^2x\), so \(0\le v\lt 1\). Then

\[f(x)^2=v(1-v)=\frac14-(v-\tfrac12)^2\le\frac14.\]

Taking non-negative square roots proves the bound; equality occurs at the stationary points.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use both product-rule terms, then eliminate sech²x.

(b)

The first factor of f′ is strictly positive for every real x.

(c)

Complete the square in tanh²x.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use a second derivative or gradient sign change.
Complete the square and deduce the bound.

\[12 q + 5=0,\qquad q=- \frac{5}{12}.\]

\[12 p^{2} y + 6 p + 3 q x + 6 q y^{2} + 6 x=0.\]

Now substitute the point and the value of \(p\):

\[21 q - \frac{204}{49}=0,\qquad q=\frac{68}{343}.\]

questions.title: An inverse tangent through an implicit relation

\[p \left(2 \tan^{2}{\left(2 y \right)} + 2\right) - 1=0.\]

Use \(1+\tan^2 2y=1+(x-1)^2\). The first relation is \(2[1+(x-1)^2]p=1\). Its derivative gives \(4(x-1)p+2[1+(x-1)^2]q=0\). Substitute \([1+(x-1)^2]^{-1}=2p\) to obtain

\[q=p^{2} \left(4 - 4 x\right).\]

The first differentiated relation gives \(p=\frac{1}{4}\). Substituting into the identity gives

\[q=- \frac{1}{4}.\]

questions.title: A zero gradient without a maximum or minimum
questions.prompt_html:
\[f(x)=\sinh^{-1}(2x)-\tan^{-1}(2x),\qquad x\in\mathbb R.\]

  1. Find \(f^{\prime}(x)\) and determine its sign.

    [3]

  2. Find the first non-zero term in the Maclaurin expansion of \(f\).

    [4]

  3. Classify the stationary point at the origin and state its tangent. Justify that the concavity changes there.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

Positive for \(x\ne0\); zero only at \(x=0\).

(b)

\(f(x)=\frac43x^3+O(x^5)\).

(c)

Stationary inflection at \((0,0)\); tangent \(y=0\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[f^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{2}{4 x^{2} + 1} + \frac{2}{\sqrt{4 x^{2} + 1}}.\]

For \(x\ne0\), \(1+4x^2\gt 1\) and its square root is smaller than itself. Therefore the first reciprocal is larger and \(f^{\prime}(x)\gt 0\). At zero \(f^{\prime}(0)=0\).

(b)

Use the local Maclaurin formula

\[f(x)=f(0)+f^{\prime}(0)x+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2!}x^2+\frac{f^{(3)}(0)}{3!}x^3+O(x^{4}).\]
\[f^{(1)}(x)=\frac{2 \left(4 x^{2} - \sqrt{4 x^{2} + 1} + 1\right)}{\left(4 x^{2} + 1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.\]
\[f^{(2)}(x)=\frac{16 x}{\left(4 x^{2} + 1\right)^{2}} - \frac{8 x}{\left(4 x^{2} + 1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.\]
\[f^{(3)}(x)=\frac{8 \left(8 x^{2} \sqrt{4 x^{2} + 1} - 24 x^{2} - \sqrt{4 x^{2} + 1} + 2\right)}{64 x^{6} + 48 x^{4} + 12 x^{2} + 1}.\]

The values at zero are

\[f^{(0)}(0)=0,\qquad f^{(1)}(0)=0,\qquad f^{(2)}(0)=0,\qquad f^{(3)}(0)=8.\]

Insert these values, dividing each derivative by its factorial:

\[f(x)=\frac{4 x^{3}}{3}+O(x^{4}).\]

Both inverse functions are odd, so the next possible non-zero power is fifth.

(c)

The positive gradient on both sides shows that the origin is neither a maximum nor a minimum. Also

\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{8x\,[2-\sqrt{1+4x^2}]}{(1+4x^2)^2}.\]

For \(|x|\lt \sqrt3/2\) the bracket is positive. Thus the second derivative changes from negative to positive at zero. The origin is a stationary point of inflection, with tangent \(y=0\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Compare a number greater than 1 with its square root.

(b)

The linear terms cancel. Compute the third derivative.

(c)

A zero first derivative does not automatically imply a turning point.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the cancellation of the constant, linear and quadratic terms.
Exclude an extremum using the gradient sign.

questions.title: Changing the independent variable by a cube
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(t=x^3\) with \(x\gt 0\), and regard \(y\) as a function of \(t\).

  1. Express \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) in terms of derivatives with respect to \(t\).

    [4]

  2. Hence transform

    \[y^{\prime\prime}-\left(\frac2x+9x^2\right)y^{\prime}+18x^4y=9x^4e^{-x^3}.\]

    into a constant-coefficient equation in \(t\).

    [3]

  3. Find the general solution in terms of \(x\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Since \(\frac{dt}{dx}=3x^2\),

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2\frac{dy}{dt}.\]

Differentiate this product with respect to \(x\):

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x\frac{dy}{dt}+9x^4\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}.\]

Equivalently replace \(x\) by \(t^{1/3}\).

(b)

Substitute the expressions from part (a):

\[6xy_t+9x^4y_{tt}-(2/x+9x^2)(3x^2y_t)+18x^4y=9x^4e^{-t}.\]

The terms \(6xy_t\) cancel. Divide by \(9x^4\gt 0\) to obtain

\[y_{tt}-3y_t+2y=e^{-t}.\]

(c)

The auxiliary equation \(m^2-3m+2=0\) has roots \(1,2\). For a particular integral \(ce^{-t}\), the multiplier is \(1+3+2=6\), so \(c=1/6\). Therefore

\[y=Ae^{x^3}+Be^{2x^3}+\frac16e^{-x^3},\qquad x\gt 0.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The factor 3x² must also be differentiated.

(b)

Collect the y_t terms before dividing.

(c)

Solve the constant-coefficient equation before substituting back.

marking_criteria.description_html: Differentiate the product and apply the chain rule again.

questions.title: Two stationary points on a hyperbola
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) has equation

\[- 9 y^{2} + \left(x + 2 y\right)^{2} + 36=0.\]

  1. Find a relation between \(x\) and \(y\) at a regular stationary point.

    [3]

  2. Find all stationary points in the stated domain.

    [3]

  3. Find the second derivative at each stationary point and determine its nature.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(2 \left(x + 2 y\right)=0\).

(b)

\((-4,2),\quad (4,-2)\).

(c)

\((-4,2)\text{, local minimum};\quad (4,-2)\text{, local maximum}\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(q=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\). Implicit differentiation gives

\[4 p x - 10 p y + 2 x + 4 y=0.\]

At a regular stationary point \(p=0\), so

\[2 \left(x + 2 y\right)=0.\]

(b)

On the requested branch, the stationary relation gives \(y=- \frac{x}{2}\). Substitute this in the original equation:

\[- \frac{9 \left(x - 4\right) \left(x + 4\right)}{4}=0.\]

Solving and substituting back gives the following admissible points:

\((-4,2)\): \(p=0\) and the coefficient of \(p\) is \(-36\), which is non-zero.

\((4,-2)\): \(p=0\) and the coefficient of \(p\) is \(36\), which is non-zero.

(c)

Differentiate the first relation again:

\[- 10 p^{2} + 8 p + 4 q x - 10 q y + 2=0.\]

At a stationary point \(p=0\). Evaluate the remaining equation separately at each point.

At \((-4,2)\),

\[2 - 36 q=0,\qquad q=\frac{1}{18}.\]

Thus this point is a local minimum.

At \((4,-2)\),

\[36 q + 2=0,\qquad q=- \frac{1}{18}.\]

Thus this point is a local maximum.

(b)

questions.title: An inverse hyperbolic function and its tangent
questions.prompt_html:
\[f(x)=x\cosh^{-1}x-\sqrt{x^2-1},\qquad x\gt 1.\]

  1. Find and simplify \(f^{\prime}(x)\) and \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)\).

    [4]

  2. Find the exact tangent at \(x=5/3\).

    [3]

  3. Find the limits of \(f(x)\), \(f^{\prime}(x)\) and \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)\) as \(x\to1^+\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The product rule gives

\[f^{\prime}(x)=\cosh^{-1}x+\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}-\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}=\cosh^{-1}x.\]

Hence \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=1/\sqrt{x^2-1}\). The positive square root is valid because \(x\gt 1\).

(b)

Here \(\cosh^{-1}(5/3)=\ln3\) and \(\sqrt{x^2-1}=4/3\). Thus the point is \((5/3,\,(5/3)\ln3-4/3)\) and the gradient is \(\ln3\). Therefore

\[y=x\ln3-\frac43.\]

(c)

Both terms in f tend to zero, so its limit is 0. Since \(f^{\prime}(x)=\cosh^{-1}x\), the first derivative tends to 0. However \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=1/\sqrt{x^2-1}\) tends to \(+\infty\). The function and first derivative have finite one-sided limits, but the second derivative does not.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Do not expand the inverse hyperbolic function before differentiating.

(b)

Use the exact logarithmic value of acosh(5/3).

(c)

Evaluate each limit from the expression valid for x>1.

marking_criteria.description_html: Differentiate acosh x and the radical correctly.
Correct infinite limit of the second derivative.

questions.title: A parameter controlling the number of intersections
questions.prompt_html:
\[f_k(x)=\cosh(2x)-k\sinh x,\qquad k\in\mathbb R.\]

  1. Show that \(f_k\) has exactly one stationary point for each real \(k\).

    [3]

  2. Find the stationary value and prove that it is the global minimum.

    [5]

  3. Determine the number of real roots of \(f_k(x)=0\) for all real \(k\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(x=\sinh^{-1}(k/4)\).

(b)

Global minimum \(1-k^2/8\).

(c)

Two if \(|k|\gt 2\sqrt2\); one if \(|k|=2\sqrt2\); none if \(|k|\lt 2\sqrt2\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The derivative is \(f_k^{\prime}(x)=\cosh x(4\sinh x-k)\). Since \(\cosh x\gt 0\) and \(\sinh x\) is strictly increasing onto the real line, the unique solution is \(x=\sinh^{-1}(k/4)\).

(b)

Before the stationary point \(4\sinh x-k\lt 0\); afterwards it is positive. Thus the function decreases and then increases. Using \(\cosh2x=1+2\sinh^2x\) gives

\[f_k\bigl(\sinh^{-1}(k/4)\bigr)=1+2\left(\frac{k}{4}\right)^2-k\left(\frac{k}{4}\right)=1-\frac{k^2}{8}.\]

Moreover \(f_k(x)\to+\infty\) at both ends of the real line because the \(e^{2|x|}\) contribution dominates the terms of order \(e^{|x|}\).

(c)

The two monotonic arms both tend to \(+\infty\). They meet at the minimum. Hence a negative minimum gives two distinct roots, a zero minimum gives one root with a horizontal tangent, and a positive minimum gives none. Compare \(1-k^2/8\) with zero.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Factor out cosh x and use its strict positivity.

(b)

Use the double-angle identity at the stationary point.

(c)

Count intersections on the two monotonic arms, including the equality case.

marking_criteria.description_html: Show the behaviour at both infinite ends.

questions.title: A stationary point that disappears at the parameter boundary
questions.prompt_html:
\[g_k(x)=\ln(\cosh x)-kx,\qquad x\in\mathbb R.\]

  1. Find the first and second derivatives and explain why any stationary point must be a minimum.

    [3]

  2. Determine exactly which \(k\) give a stationary point. Describe the monotonicity when there is no stationary point.

    [5]

  3. For \(k=3/5\), find the exact coordinates of the minimum and its tangent.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(g_k^{\prime}=\tanh x-k,\quad g_k^{\prime\prime}=\operatorname{sech}^2x\).

(b)

Stationary point iff \(|k|\lt 1\). Strictly decreasing for \(k\ge1\) and increasing for \(k\le-1\).

(c)

\((\ln2,\,\ln(5/4)-(3/5)\ln2)\); tangent \(y=\ln(5/4)-(3/5)\ln2\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[g_k^{\prime}(x)=\tanh x-k,\qquad g_k^{\prime\prime}(x)=\operatorname{sech}^2x\gt 0.\]

A zero first derivative therefore gives a strict local minimum; the strict increase of the first derivative makes it unique.

(b)

The range of \(\tanh x\) is \((-1,1)\), with endpoints never attained. Hence a stationary point exists exactly when \(|k|\lt 1\), and then \(x=\tanh^{-1}k\). For \(k\ge1\) the first derivative is strictly negative everywhere. For \(k\le-1\) it is strictly positive everywhere. There is no stationary point at the boundary values \(k=\pm1\).

(c)

Since \(\tanh(\ln2)=3/5\), the minimum occurs at \(x=\ln2\). Also \(\cosh(\ln2)=5/4\). The minimum value is \(\ln(5/4)-(3/5)\ln2\), and the tangent is horizontal at that height.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate ln(cosh x) as a logarithmic composition.

(b)

The endpoints of the range of tanh are not attained at finite x.

(c)

Evaluate the inverse tanh using its logarithmic expression.

questions.title: A cycloidal curve and excluded parameters
questions.prompt_html:
\[x=6 t - 3 \sin{\left(2 t \right)},\quad y=2 - 2 \cos{\left(2 t \right)},\quad -\pi\le t\le\pi.\]

  1. Show that \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac23\cot t\) wherever it exists as a finite derivative. State all exceptional parameter values.

    [4]

  2. Find the exact value of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) when \(t=\pi/6\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=6 - 6 \cos{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=4 \sin{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2 \cot{\left(t \right)}}{3}.\]

Here \(\frac{dx}{dt}=12\sin^2t\). It vanishes at \(t=-\pi,0,\pi\) in the stated interval. The quotient cannot be used at these cusp parameters, and \(\cot t\) has no finite limit there.

(b)

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=- \frac{2 \left(\cot^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 1\right)}{3}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=- \frac{1}{18 \sin^{4}{\left(t \right)}}.\]

At \(t=\pi/6\), this gives \(-8/9\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Check zeros of dx/dt before cancelling trigonometric factors.

(b)

Divide the derivative of cot t by dx/dt.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find all zeros of dx/dt in the interval.

questions.title: Concavity on a monotonic parametric branch
questions.prompt_html:
\[x=- t^{2} + 6 t,\quad y=2 - 2 e^{- t},\quad 0\le t\lt 3.\]

  1. Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) in terms of \(t\).

    [5]

  2. Find the point of inflection and justify your answer.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=6 - 2 t,\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=2 e^{- t}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{e^{- t}}{3 - t}.\]

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=\frac{\left(t - 2\right) e^{- t}}{\left(t - 3\right)^{2}}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\left(t - 2\right) e^{- t}}{2 \left(3 - t\right)^{3}}.\]

(b)

On \(0\le t\lt 3\), \(\frac{dx}{dt}=6-2t\gt 0\), so increasing \(t\) also increases \(x\). The denominator and exponential factor in the second derivative are positive; its sign changes from negative to positive at \(t=2\). The point is \((8,2-2e^{-2})\).
questions.hint_html:

(b)

questions.title: A product substitution with a shifted variable
questions.prompt_html:
For \(x\gt -1\), a function satisfies

\[(x+1)^2y^{\prime\prime}+[(x+1)^2+4(x+1)]y^{\prime}+[2+2(x+1)-2(x+1)^2]y=6\sin x-2\cos x.\]

  1. Use \(w=(x+1)^2y\) to show that \(w^{\prime\prime}+w^{\prime}-2w=6\sin x-2\cos x\).

    [4]

  2. Find the general solution for \(y\).

    [7]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[w^{\prime}=(x+1)^2y^{\prime}+2(x+1)y,\]
\[w^{\prime\prime}=(x+1)^2y^{\prime\prime}+4(x+1)y^{\prime}+2y.\]

Adding \(w^{\prime}\) and subtracting \(2w\) reproduces every coefficient on the given left-hand side.

(b)

The auxiliary equation is \(m^2+m-2=(m-1)(m+2)=0\). Thus \(w_c=Ae^x+Be^{-2x}\). Put \(w_p=c\sin x+d\cos x\). Substitution yields sine and cosine coefficients \(-3c-d\) and \(c-3d\). Equating them with \(6\) and \(-2\) gives \(c=-2,d=0\). Therefore

\[w=Ae^x+Be^{-2x}-2\sin x,\qquad y=\frac{Ae^x+Be^{-2x}-2\sin x}{(x+1)^2}.\]

The denominator is non-zero on the stated domain.

(b)

questions.title: A monotonic combination of coth and cosech
questions.prompt_html:
\[f(x)=\coth x-2\operatorname{cosech}x,\qquad x\gt 0.\]

  1. Differentiate and prove that \(f\) is strictly increasing.

    [3]

  2. Find the limits as \(x\to0^+\) and \(x\to\infty\). Hence state the range.

    [3]

  3. Find the exact zero of \(f\) and justify its uniqueness.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[f^{\prime}=-\operatorname{cosech}^2x+2\operatorname{cosech}x\coth x=\frac{2\cosh x-1}{\sinh^2x}.\]

For \(x\gt 0\), \(\cosh x\gt 1\) and \(\sinh^2x\gt 0\), so the derivative is strictly positive.

(b)

Write \(f=(\cosh x-2)/\sinh x\). As \(x\to0^+\), the numerator tends to \(-1\) and the denominator tends to zero from above, giving \(-\infty\). In exponential form, division by \(e^x\) gives the limit \(1\) at infinity. By continuity and strict increase, the range is \((-\infty,1)\).

(c)

The denominator is non-zero, so \(f=0\) gives \(\cosh x=2\). Therefore \(x=\ln(2+\sqrt3)\). The other solution of the unrestricted cosh equation is negative and is excluded; strict increase proves uniqueness on the given domain.

questions.title: One conic, two kinds of tangent and a local expansion
questions.prompt_html:
\[x^2+2xy+4y^2=4.\]

  1. Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \((0,1)\).

    [4]

  2. Find the Maclaurin expansion through \(x^2\) of the branch through \((0,1)\).

    [3]

  3. Find all points with horizontal tangents and classify them as stationary points of their local branches.

    [4]

  4. Find all points with vertical tangents.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

With \(p=y^{\prime}\) and \(q=y^{\prime\prime}\), differentiating once and twice gives

\[2x+2y+(2x+8y)p=0,\]
\[2+4p+8p^2+(2x+8y)q=0.\]

At \((0,1)\) these give \(p=-1/4\) and \(2-1+1/2+8q=0\), hence \(q=-3/16\).

(b)

The branch has \(y(0)=1\). Insert the two derivatives into the Maclaurin formula:

\[y=1-\frac14x-\frac{3}{32}x^2+O(x^3).\]

The other branch passes through \((0,-1)\) and must not be used.

(c)

For a horizontal tangent, \(p=0\) gives \(x=-y\). The curve then gives \(3y^2=4\). Thus the points are \((-2/\sqrt3,2/\sqrt3)\) and \((2/\sqrt3,-2/\sqrt3)\). At them \(q=-1/(3y)\), so the first is a local maximum and the second a local minimum.

(d)

A vertical tangent occurs when \(2x+8y=0\) but \(2x+2y\ne0\). Thus \(x=-4y\) and the curve gives \(12y^2=4\). The points are \((-4/\sqrt3,1/\sqrt3)\) and \((4/\sqrt3,-1/\sqrt3)\). At both points the numerator is non-zero.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the twice-differentiated relation, retaining all product terms.

(b)

The given point selects one of the two branches.

(c)

Set the numerator to zero and check that the denominator is non-zero.

(d)

Exchange the roles of x and y to justify a vertical tangent.

questions.title: The three parameter regimes of an inverse-hyperbolic curve
questions.prompt_html:
\[f_k(x)=\sinh^{-1}(kx)-x,\qquad k\gt 0.\]

  1. Find the first and second derivatives.

    [3]

  2. For \(k\ne1\), determine the number and nature of stationary points, giving their \(x\)-coordinates.

    [5]

  3. For \(k=1\), classify the origin and find the first non-zero Maclaurin term.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\frac{k}{\sqrt{k^{2} x^{2} + 1}} - 1\) and \(- \frac{k^{3} x}{\left(k^{2} x^{2} + 1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\).

(b)

None for \(0\lt k\lt 1\). For \(k\gt 1\): minimum at \(-\sqrt{k^2-1}/k\), maximum at \(\sqrt{k^2-1}/k\).

(c)

Stationary inflection; \(-x^3/6+O(x^5)\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[f_k^{\prime}(x)=\frac{k}{\sqrt{k^{2} x^{2} + 1}} - 1.\]
\[f_k^{\prime\prime}(x)=- \frac{k^{3} x}{\left(k^{2} x^{2} + 1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.\]

(b)

The stationary equation is \(\sqrt{1+k^2x^2}=k\). Both sides are non-negative and \(k\gt 0\), so squaring is valid and gives \(k^2x^2=k^2-1\). If \(0\lt k\lt 1\) this has no real solution. If \(k\gt 1\) there are two: \(x=\pm\sqrt{k^2-1}/k\). The sign of the second derivative is opposite to the sign of \(x\), so the negative point is a local minimum and the positive point a local maximum.

(c)

Now \(f^{\prime}(x)=1/\sqrt{1+x^2}-1\), which is negative for \(x\ne0\) and zero at zero. The second derivative \(-x/(1+x^2)^{3/2}\) changes from positive to negative. Thus the origin is a stationary inflection, not an extremum. At zero \(f(0)=f^{\prime}(0)=f^{\prime\prime}(0)=0\) and \(f^{(3)}(0)=-1\), giving

\[f(x)=-\frac16x^3+O(x^5).\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Apply the chain rule with the factor k.

(b)

The square-root equation already constrains the parameter.

(c)

Treat the boundary parameter separately rather than merging two extrema.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the zero gradient but no extremum.

questions.title: A positive branch of a cubic loop
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) has equation

\[x^{3} - 6 x y + 2 y^{3}=0.\]

Restrict attention to \(x\gt 0,\ y\gt 0\).

  1. Find a relation between \(x\) and \(y\) at a regular stationary point.

    [3]

  2. Find all stationary points in the stated domain.

    [5]

  3. Find the second derivative at each stationary point and determine its nature.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(q=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\). Implicit differentiation gives

\[- 6 p x + 6 p y^{2} + 3 x^{2} - 6 y=0.\]

At a regular stationary point \(p=0\), so

\[3 \left(x^{2} - 2 y\right)=0.\]

(b)

On the requested branch, the stationary relation gives \(y=\frac{x^{2}}{2}\). Substitute this in the original equation:

\[\frac{x^{3} \left(x - 2\right) \left(x^{2} + 2 x + 4\right)}{4}=0.\]

Discard \(x=0\) because it is excluded by the stated domain.

Solving and substituting back gives the following admissible points:

\((2,2)\): \(p=0\) and the coefficient of \(p\) is \(12\), which is non-zero.

(c)

Differentiate the first relation again:

\[12 p^{2} y - 12 p - 6 q x + 6 q y^{2} + 6 x=0.\]

At a stationary point \(p=0\). Evaluate the remaining equation separately at each point.

At \((2,2)\),

\[12 q + 12=0,\qquad q=-1.\]

Thus this point is a local maximum.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Set y′=0 only after obtaining the full derivative relation.

(b)

Substitute the relation from part (a) into the curve and retain every permitted root.

(c)

Differentiate before putting the first derivative equal to zero.

marking_criteria.description_html: Set the first derivative to zero on a regular branch.
Find all admissible stationary points and exclude any prohibited ones.
Differentiate the first relation a second time.

questions.title: A cubic relation involving the first derivative
questions.prompt_html:
A twice-differentiable real function satisfies

\[p^{3} + x^{2} + 2 y^{2} - 36=0,\qquad y(1)=-2,\]

where \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\).

  1. Find \(y^{\prime}(1)\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(y^{\prime\prime}(1)\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Substitution gives

\[p^{3} - 27=0.\]

The real cubic root is \(p=3\).

(b)

Differentiate the relation, remembering that \(dp/dx=q=y^{\prime\prime}\):

\[3 p^{2} q + 4 p y + 2 x=0.\]

At the stated point,

\[27 q - 22=0,\qquad q=\frac{22}{27}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the real cube root; no choice of sign is introduced.

(b)

The derivative of a bracket containing y′ also contains y″.

marking_criteria.description_html: Substitute the initial point and first derivative.

questions.title: A square substitution and a positive solution branch
questions.prompt_html:
For \(x\ge0\), a positive function \(y\) satisfies

\[2yy^{\prime\prime}+2(y^{\prime})^2+6yy^{\prime}+2y^2=2x+3,\qquad y(0)=2,\quad y^{\prime}(0)=-\frac14.\]

  1. Put \(w=y^2\) and derive a linear differential equation for \(w\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(y\) satisfying the initial data.

    [7]

  3. Show that \(y/\sqrt{x}\to1\) as \(x\to\infty\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[w^{\prime}=2yy^{\prime},\qquad w^{\prime\prime}=2(y^{\prime})^2+2yy^{\prime\prime}.\]

Substitution gives

\[w^{\prime\prime}+3w^{\prime}+2w=2x+3.\]

(b)

The auxiliary roots are \(-1,-2\). A trial \(cx+d\) gives \(c=1,d=0\). Hence \(w=Ae^{-x}+Be^{-2x}+x\). The initial data become \(w(0)=4\) and \(w^{\prime}(0)=2(2)(-1/4)=-1\). Thus \(A+B=4\) and \(-A-2B+1=-1\), giving \(A=6,B=-2\). The positive branch is

\[y=\sqrt{x+6e^{-x}-2e^{-2x}}.\]

For \(x\ge0\), \(6e^{-x}-2e^{-2x}=2e^{-x}(3-e^{-x})\gt 0\), so this branch remains real and positive.

(c)

For \(x\gt 0\),

\[\frac{y}{\sqrt x}=\sqrt{1+\frac{6e^{-x}-2e^{-2x}}x}.\]

The exponential terms divided by \(x\) tend to zero. Continuity of the positive square root gives the limit 1.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The second derivative of y² contains two terms.

(b)

Translate y′(0) into w′(0) before solving for constants.

(c)

Compare the square of y with x before taking the limit.

marking_criteria.description_html: Form the ratio inside a square root.
Show the added term tends to zero.

questions.title: Mixed products with different powers
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[2 x^{2} y + 3 x y^{2} + 8=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(-1,2)\).

  1. Use implicit differentiation to find the exact value of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at \(P\).

    [3]

  2. Find the exact value of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(P\).

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\). Differentiate the complete equation with respect to \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\):

\[2 p x^{2} + 6 p x y + 4 x y + 3 y^{2}=0.\]

At \(P\) this becomes

\[4 - 10 p=0,\qquad p=\frac{2}{5}.\]

(b)

Differentiate the first relation before substituting the point. With \(q=\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), the product and chain rules give

\[6 p^{2} x + 8 p x + 12 p y + 2 q x^{2} + 6 q x y + 4 y=0.\]

Now substitute the point and the value of \(p\):

\[\frac{336}{25} - 10 q=0,\qquad q=\frac{168}{125}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate products before substituting the coordinates.

(b)

Differentiate the relation from part (a), not the numerical gradient.

marking_criteria.description_html: Retain all product-rule terms, including squared first derivatives.
Substitute the point and the first derivative only after differentiation.

questions.title: Recovering an inverse-sine function from derivatives
questions.prompt_html:
A function has the form \(f(x)=a\sin^{-1}(x/b)+c\), where \(a\gt 0\), \(b\gt 0\) and \(c\) is real. It satisfies

\[f(0)=1,\qquad f^{\prime}(0)=2,\qquad f^{(3)}(0)=\frac12.\]

  1. Find \(a,b,c\).

    [5]

  2. State the real domain of \(f\) and find its second derivative on the interior.

    [3]

  3. Find the tangent at \(x=1\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

At zero \(c=1\). Differentiation gives \(f^{\prime}=a/\sqrt{b^2-x^2}\) and \(f^{\prime\prime}=ax(b^2-x^2)^{-3/2}\). Hence \(f^{\prime}(0)=a/b=2\) and \(f^{(3)}(0)=a/b^3=1/2\). Dividing gives \(b^2=4\). The positive root is \(b=2\), and \(a=4\).

(b)

The inverse sine is real when \(|x/2|\le1\), so the domain is \([-2,2]\). The finite differentiable interior is \((-2,2)\), where

\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{4 x}{\left(4 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.\]

(c)

The point is \((1,1+2\pi/3)\) and its gradient is \(4/\sqrt3\). Thus

\[y=1+\frac{2\pi}{3}+\frac4{\sqrt3}(x-1).\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the first and third derivatives at zero to remove the scale factor.

(b)

The endpoints belong to the function domain but not to the finite-derivative formula.

(c)

Evaluate both the function and its gradient.

questions.title: A cubic relation with unequal weights
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x^{3} - 2 x y - 4 y^{3}=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(2,1)\).

  1. Use implicit differentiation to find the exact value of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at \(P\).

    [3]

  2. Find the exact value of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(P\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\). Differentiate the complete equation with respect to \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\):

\[- 2 p x - 12 p y^{2} + 3 x^{2} - 2 y=0.\]

At \(P\) this becomes

\[10 - 16 p=0,\qquad p=\frac{5}{8}.\]

(b)

Differentiate the first relation before substituting the point. With \(q=\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), the product and chain rules give

\[- 24 p^{2} y - 4 p - 2 q x - 12 q y^{2} + 6 x=0.\]

Now substitute the point and the value of \(p\):

\[\frac{1}{8} - 16 q=0,\qquad q=\frac{1}{128}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate products before substituting the coordinates.

(b)

Differentiate the relation from part (a), not the numerical gradient.

marking_criteria.description_html: Retain all product-rule terms, including squared first derivatives.
Substitute the point and the first derivative only after differentiation.

questions.title: A logarithmic curve just touching the axis
questions.prompt_html:
\[g_a(x)=\ln(1+ae^x)-\frac23x,\qquad a\gt 0,\quad x\in\mathbb R.\]

  1. Find the first two derivatives and show that the second is positive.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact global minimum in terms of \(a\).

    [5]

  3. Find the value of \(a\) for which the \(x\)-axis is tangent to the curve.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[g_a^{\prime}(x)=\frac{ae^x}{1+ae^x}-\frac23,\qquad g_a^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{ae^x}{(1+ae^x)^2}\gt 0.\]

The sign follows from \(a\gt 0\) and \(e^x\gt 0\).

(b)

Set the first derivative to zero: \(3ae^x=2(1+ae^x)\), so \(ae^x=2\) and \(x=\ln(2/a)\). The strictly increasing gradient is negative before and positive after this point. Therefore the minimum is global and equals

\[\ln3-\frac23\ln(2/a).\]

(c)

The minimum must be zero. Hence \(\ln(2/a)=\frac32\ln3\) and \(2/a=3\sqrt3\). Therefore \(a=2/(3\sqrt3)\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate the logarithm and then its rational derivative.

(b)

Solve first for ae^x, then recover x.

(c)

A horizontal contact with the axis occurs at the minimum.

questions.title: A logarithmic change of independent variable
questions.prompt_html:
For \(x\gt -2\),

\[(x+2)^2y^{\prime\prime}-(x+2)y^{\prime}-3y=5(x+2)^2,\qquad y(-1)=0,\quad y^{\prime}(-1)=1.\]

  1. Put \(u=\ln(x+2)\) and transform the differential equation into an equation in \(u\).

    [4]

  2. Find the general solution in terms of \(x\).

    [5]

  3. Use the initial data to find the particular solution.

    [3]

  4. Find \(\lim_{x\to\infty}y/x^3\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Because \(du/dx=1/(x+2)\),

\[y_x=\frac{y_u}{x+2},\qquad y_{xx}=\frac{y_{uu}-y_u}{(x+2)^2}.\]

Substitution gives

\[y_{uu}-2y_u-3y=5e^{2u}.\]

(b)

The auxiliary equation is \((m-3)(m+1)=0\). For \(ce^{2u}\), substitution gives \((4-4-3)c=5\), so \(c=-5/3\). Thus

\[y=A(x+2)^3+\frac{B}{x+2}-\frac53(x+2)^2.\]

(c)

At \(x=-1\), \(x+2=1\). The equations are \(A+B=5/3\) and \(3A-B=13/3\). Solving gives \(A=3/2,B=1/6\).

(d)

Divide each term by \(x^3\). The cubic term tends to \(3/2\) and the other terms tend to zero.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The second derivative includes a derivative of 1/(x+2).

(b)

Solve the transformed equation before substituting e^u=x+2.

(c)

Differentiate with respect to x when using the stated y′ datum.

(d)

Identify the leading power after expanding or taking ratios.

marking_criteria.description_html: Divide by x³ and identify the leading contribution.

questions.title: Second derivative on a parametric ellipse
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x=4 \sin{\left(3 t \right)},\qquad y=2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)},\qquad 0\lt t\lt \frac\pi3.\]

  1. Find the exact gradient at \(t=\frac{\pi}{4}\).

    [3]

  2. Find the exact second derivative at the same point.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=12 \cos{\left(3 t \right)},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=- 6 \sin{\left(3 t \right)}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=- \frac{\tan{\left(3 t \right)}}{2}.\]

At \(t=\frac{\pi}{4}\), the gradient is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

(b)

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=- \frac{3 \left(\tan^{2}{\left(3 t \right)} + 1\right)}{2}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=- \frac{1}{8 \cos^{3}{\left(3 t \right)}}.\]

At \(t=\frac{\pi}{4}\), the second derivative is \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use dy/dx=(dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

(b)

A second derivative requires a second division by dx/dt.

marking_criteria.description_html: Divide dy/dt by dx/dt and obtain the correct result.
Differentiate the gradient with respect to t.
Divide by dx/dt, rather than by dy/dt.

questions.title: The absolute value hidden by a principal inverse
questions.prompt_html:
\[f(x)=\cosh^{-1}(1+x^2),\qquad x\in\mathbb R,\]

where \(\cosh^{-1}\) denotes the non-negative principal value.

  1. Show that \(f(x)=2\sinh^{-1}(|x|/\sqrt2)\).

    [4]

  2. Find the first and second derivatives separately for \(x\gt 0\) and \(x\lt 0\).

    [4]

  3. Find the two one-sided derivatives at zero and decide whether \(f\) is differentiable there.

    [3]

  4. Explain why the usual derivative-based Maclaurin expansion cannot be applied to \(f\) at zero.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(2\sinh^{-1}(|x|/\sqrt2)\).

(b)

First derivative has the two signs above; \(f^{\prime\prime}=-2|x|/(x^2+2)^{3/2}\).

(c)

Left \(-\sqrt2\), right \(\sqrt2\); not differentiable.

(d)

No two-sided Maclaurin representation; the leading term is \(\sqrt2|x|\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(u=\sinh^{-1}(|x|/\sqrt2)\ge0\). Then \(\cosh(2u)=1+2\sinh^2u=1+x^2\). Since \(2u\ge0\), it is the principal inverse-cosh value. Thus \(f=2u\).

(b)

For \(x\gt 0\), differentiate \(2\sinh^{-1}(x/\sqrt2)\). For \(x\lt 0\), differentiate \(2\sinh^{-1}(-x/\sqrt2)\). The results are

\[f^{\prime}(x)=\begin{cases}2/\sqrt{x^2+2},&x\gt 0,\\-2/\sqrt{x^2+2},&x\lt 0,\end{cases}\]
\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=-\frac{2|x|}{(x^2+2)^{3/2}},\qquad x\ne0.\]

(c)

Since \(f(0)=0\) and \(\sinh^{-1}u/u\to1\) as \(u\to0\) (from the derivative of \(\sinh^{-1}u\) at zero), the right difference quotient tends to \(\sqrt2\) and the left to \(-\sqrt2\). They differ, so there is no derivative at zero.

(d)

The Maclaurin formula requires the derivatives at zero. Here even the first derivative at zero does not exist, so the usual derivative-based expansion is unavailable. The leading behaviour is \(\sqrt2|x|\), not a single linear term valid on both sides.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The principal inverse cosh cannot return a negative value.

(b)

Handle the derivative of |x| separately on each side.

(c)

Use a difference quotient at zero; the off-zero formula cannot simply be substituted.

(d)

The obstruction already occurs at the first derivative.

marking_criteria.description_html: Explain that the usual Maclaurin formula needs derivatives at zero.
Use the unequal one-sided derivatives to rule it out.

questions.title: An implicit product of two factors
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[\left(x + 2 y\right) \left(x^{2} + y^{2}\right) - 2=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(0,1)\).

  1. Use implicit differentiation to find the exact value of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at \(P\).

    [3]

  2. Find the exact value of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(P\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\). Differentiate the complete equation with respect to \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\):

\[2 p x^{2} + 2 p x y + 6 p y^{2} + 3 x^{2} + 4 x y + y^{2}=0.\]

At \(P\) this becomes

\[6 p + 1=0,\qquad p=- \frac{1}{6}.\]

(b)

Differentiate the first relation before substituting the point. With \(q=\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), the product and chain rules give

\[2 p^{2} x + 12 p^{2} y + 8 p x + 4 p y + 2 q x^{2} + 2 q x y + 6 q y^{2} + 6 x + 4 y=0.\]

Now substitute the point and the value of \(p\):

\[6 q + \frac{11}{3}=0,\qquad q=- \frac{11}{18}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate products before substituting the coordinates.

(b)

Differentiate the relation from part (a), not the numerical gradient.

marking_criteria.description_html: Retain all product-rule terms, including squared first derivatives.
Substitute the point and the first derivative only after differentiation.

questions.title: A stationary point specified by a unique transcendental root
questions.prompt_html:
\[f_k(x)=x\operatorname{sech}(kx),\qquad k\gt 0.\]

  1. Find \(f_k^{\prime}(x)\) and show that a positive stationary point satisfies \(u\tanh u=1\), where \(u=kx\).

    [3]

  2. Prove that this equation has exactly one positive root \(u=\alpha\) and verify \(1.19\lt \alpha\lt 1.20\).

    [4]

  3. Find both stationary points in terms of \(k\) and \(\alpha\), and classify them.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[f_k^{\prime}(x)=\left(- k x \tanh{\left(k x \right)} + 1\right) \operatorname{sech}{\left(k x \right)}.\]

The sech factor is positive. Thus the stationary equation is \(kx\tanh(kx)=1\).

(b)

Let \(H(u)=u\tanh u\) for \(u\gt 0\). Then \(H^{\prime}(u)=\tanh u+u\operatorname{sech}^2u\gt 0\). Also \(H(0)=0\) and \(H(u)\to\infty\). Continuity and strict increase give exactly one crossing of 1. Numerically, \(H(1.19)-1\approx-0.011611146\) and \(H(1.20)-1\approx0.00038552841\).

(c)

The function \(u\tanh u\) is even, so the two stationary parameters are \(\pm\alpha\). The points are \((\alpha/k,\,\alpha\operatorname{sech}\alpha/k)\) and its negative. The derivative is positive between them and negative outside. Thus the negative point is a local minimum and the positive point a local maximum.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Factor out sech(kx).

(b)

Separate existence, uniqueness and the numerical bracket.

(c)

Use the symmetry of u tanh u, not of f itself.

marking_criteria.description_html: Correct opposite signs at the bracket endpoints.

questions.title: A resonant term after an exponential substitution
questions.prompt_html:
For \(x\gt 0\), the function \(y\) satisfies

\[x^2y^{\prime\prime}+2xy^{\prime}-6y=10x^2.\]

  1. With \(x=e^u\), show that \(xy_x=y_u\) and \(x^2y_{xx}=y_{uu}-y_u\).

    [3]

  2. Transform the differential equation and find its complementary function.

    [3]

  3. A suitable particular integral has the form \(cu e^{2u}\). Determine \(c\) and find the general solution in terms of \(x\).

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Since \(du/dx=1/x\), \(y_x=y_u/x\). Differentiating once more gives \(y_{xx}=(y_{uu}-y_u)/x^2\).

(b)

Substitution yields \(y_{uu}+y_u-6y=10e^{2u}\). The auxiliary equation is \((m-2)(m+3)=0\), so \(y_c=Ae^{2u}+Be^{-3u}\).

(c)

For \(y_p=cu e^{2u}\),

\[(y_p)_u=c(1+2u)e^{2u},\qquad (y_p)_{uu}=c(4+4u)e^{2u}.\]

Thus \((y_p)_{uu}+(y_p)_u-6y_p=5ce^{2u}\). Equating this with \(10e^{2u}\) gives \(c=2\). Therefore

\[y=Ax^2+Bx^{-3}+2x^2\ln x,\qquad x\gt 0.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate y_u/x using both the product and chain rules.

(b)

The forcing exponential repeats one of the complementary-function exponents.

(c)

Differentiate the supplied trial form instead of guessing an unsupported form.

questions.title: Recovering a point from its second derivative
questions.prompt_html:
The curve has parametric equations

\[x=\tanh^2t+2\ln(\operatorname{sech}t),\qquad y=3+3\tanh^4t,\qquad t\gt 0.\]

  1. Starting with exponential definitions, prove \(\tanh^2t+\operatorname{sech}^2t=1\).

    [3]

  2. Show that \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-6\operatorname{sech}^2t\).

    [4]

  3. Find the exact coordinates of the point where \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{32}{3}\).

    [7]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

The identity is established by expanding the exponential numerator.

(b)

\(- 6 \operatorname{sech}^{2}{\left(t \right)}\).

(c)

\((9/25+\ln(16/25),\ 2118/625)\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

From the exponential definitions,

\[\tanh^2t+\operatorname{sech}^2t=\frac{(e^t-e^{-t})^2+4}{(e^t+e^{-t})^2}=\frac{e^{2t}+2+e^{-2t}}{e^{2t}+2+e^{-2t}}=1.\]

(b)

Using the identity from part (a),

\[x_t=2\tanh t\operatorname{sech}^2t-2\tanh t=-2\tanh^3t,\]
\[y_t=12\tanh^3t\operatorname{sech}^2t.\]

Because \(t\gt 0\), \(\tanh t\ne0\). Dividing yields \(y_x=-6\operatorname{sech}^2t\).

(c)

Differentiate the result in part (b) and divide by \(x_t\):

\[y_{xx}=\frac{12\operatorname{sech}^2t\tanh t}{-2\tanh^3t}=-\frac{6\operatorname{sech}^2t}{\tanh^2t}.\]

Let \(v=\tanh^2t\). The prescribed value gives \(6(1-v)/v=32/3\), so \(v=9/25\). Since \(t\gt 0\), \(\tanh t=3/5\) and \(\operatorname{sech}t=4/5\). Substitution in the original parametrisation gives

\[\boxed{\left(\frac9{25}+\ln\frac{16}{25},\ \frac{2118}{625}\right)}.\]

There is only one such positive parameter because tanh is strictly increasing.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Write both functions over the denominator (e^t+e^(−t))².

(b)

Simplify x_t using the identity before dividing.

(c)

Use v=tanh²t, and select the positive square root from t>0.

questions.title: An exponential parametric curve
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x=t + e^{- t},\qquad y=t - e^{- t},\qquad t\gt 0.\]

  1. Find the exact gradient at \(t=\ln{\left(3 \right)}\).

    [3]

  2. Find the exact second derivative at the same point.

questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=1 - e^{- t},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=1 + e^{- t}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1 + e^{- t}}{1 - e^{- t}}.\]

At \(t=\ln{\left(3 \right)}\), the gradient is \(2\).

(b)

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=- \frac{2 e^{t}}{\left(e^{t} - 1\right)^{2}}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=- \frac{2 e^{- t}}{\left(1 - e^{- t}\right)^{3}}.\]

At \(t=\ln{\left(3 \right)}\), the second derivative is \(- \frac{9}{4}\).

(a)

Use dy/dx=(dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

A second derivative requires a second division by dx/dt.

questions.prompt_html:
\[x=\frac{t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - 3 \sqrt{t},\quad y=2 t - 1,\quad 0\lt t\le5.\]

  1. Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and locate the vertical tangent.

    [4]

  3. Find the set of parameter values for which \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\gt 0\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2} - \frac{3}{2 \sqrt{t}},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=2.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4 \sqrt{t}}{t - 3}.\]

At \(t=3\), \(\frac{dx}{dt}=0\) but \(\frac{dy}{dt}\ne0\). The tangent is vertical at \((- 2 \sqrt{3},5)\).

(b)

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=- \frac{2 \left(t + 3\right)}{\sqrt{t} \left(t - 3\right)^{2}}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{- 4 t - 12}{\left(t - 3\right)^{3}}.\]

(c)

Every factor in the numerator has the displayed fixed sign on the domain. The cubed denominator changes sign at \(t=3\). Hence the second derivative is positive for \(0\lt t\lt 3\). It is undefined at the vertical tangent; that point cannot be classified as an ordinary stationary point by setting \(\frac{dy}{dx}=0\).

(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=2 t - \frac{2}{t},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=3.\]

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3 t}{2 t^{2} - 2}.\]

(b)

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

questions.title: Recovering a parametrisation from derivative data
questions.prompt_html:
\[x=t+\frac13t^3,\qquad y=at^2+b\ln t,\qquad t\gt 0.\]

At \(t=1\), \(\frac{dy}{dx}=3\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-1\).

  1. Find \(a\) and \(b\).

    [5]

  2. For these values, find the second derivative in terms of \(t\) and show that the curve has no point of inflection.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a=2,\ b=2\).

(b)

\(- \frac{2 \left(2 t^{4} + t^{2} + 1\right)}{t^{2} \left(t^{2} + 1\right)^{3}}\); no inflection for \(t\gt 0\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2 a t^{2} + b}{t^{3} + t}.\]

At \(t=1\) the gradient is \(a+b/2\). Using \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=(y_{tt}x_t-y_tx_{tt})/(x_t)^3\) gives \(-b/2\) at \(t=1\). Thus \(b=2\) and \(a=2\).

(b)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=t^{2} + 1,\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=4 t + \frac{2}{t}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2 \left(2 t^{2} + 1\right)}{t \left(t^{2} + 1\right)}.\]

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=- \frac{2 \left(2 t^{4} + t^{2} + 1\right)}{t^{2} \left(t^{2} + 1\right)^{2}}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=- \frac{2 \left(2 t^{4} + t^{2} + 1\right)}{t^{2} \left(t^{2} + 1\right)^{3}}.\]

Equivalently, the second derivative is \(-\dfrac{2(2t^4+t^2+1)}{t^2(1+t^2)^3}\). Every factor in its denominator is positive and the numerator is strictly negative for \(t\gt 0\). Since \(\frac{dx}{dt}=1+t^2\gt 0\), the curve is a single regular branch and has no inflection.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the parametric second-derivative formula before substituting t=1.

(b)

Prove a strict sign, not merely the absence of a guessed root.

questions.prompt_html:

(a)

\(y_x=3\cos2t/\cos t,\\ y_{xx}=-3\sin t(1+2\cos^2t)/(2\cos^3t)\); exclude \(t=\pi/2\).

(b)

\((\sqrt2,3),\quad(\sqrt2,-3)\).

questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[ rac{dx}{dt}=2 \cos{\left(t ight)},\qquad rac{dy}{dt}=6 \cos{\left(2 t ight)}.\]

Where \( rac{dx}{dt} e0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[ rac{d^2y}{dx^2}= rac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx} ight)}{ rac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[ rac{d}{dt}\left( rac{dy}{dx} ight)= rac{3 \left(\sin{\left(t ight)} \cos{\left(2 t ight)} - 2 \sin{\left(2 t ight)} \cos{\left(t ight)} ight)}{\cos^{2}{\left(t ight)}}.\]

questions.title: From a hyperbolic parameter to a local expansion
questions.prompt_html:
A curve is defined for real \(t\) by

\[x=\tanh t,\qquad y=\ln(\cosh t).\]

  1. Eliminate \(t\) and state the exact range of \(x\).

    [3]

  2. Using the parametric equations, find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), expressing both in terms of \(x\).

    [4]

  3. Find the Maclaurin expansion through the term in \(x^4\).

    [3]

  4. Show that the curve has a unique global minimum, and give its coordinates.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(y=-\tfrac12\ln(1-x^2),\quad -1\lt x\lt 1\).

(b)

\(y_x=x/(1-x^2),\quad y_{xx}=(1+x^2)/(1-x^2)^2\).

(c)

\(\frac{x^{4}}{4} + \frac{x^{2}}{2}\)\(+O(x^6)\).

(d)

\((0,0)\) is the unique global minimum.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The identity \(1-\tanh^2t=\operatorname{sech}^2t\) gives \(\cosh^2t=1/(1-x^2)\). Since \(\cosh t\gt 0\),

\[y=-\frac12\ln(1-x^2),\qquad -1\lt x\lt 1.\]

The endpoints are not reached at finite real t.

(b)

\[x_t=\operatorname{sech}^2t,\qquad y_t=\tanh t,\qquad y_x=\frac{\tanh t}{\operatorname{sech}^2t}=\frac{x}{1-x^2}.\]

A second parametric differentiation yields

\[y_{xx}=\frac{\cosh2t}{\operatorname{sech}^2t}=\frac{1+x^2}{(1-x^2)^2}.\]

Here \(\cosh2t=(1+x^2)/(1-x^2)\).

(c)

Use \(\ln(1-z)=-z-z^2/2+O(z^3)\) with \(z=x^2\). Hence

\[y=\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^4}{4}+O(x^6).\]

(d)

The denominator of \(y_x=x/(1-x^2)\) is positive. Thus y decreases for x<0 and increases for x>0. Its only minimum is \((0,0)\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use cosh²t=1/(1−tanh²t) and its positive square root.

(b)

Do not confuse d/dt with d/dx in the second step.

(c)

(d)

Use the sign of the first derivative over the entire domain.

questions.title: A stationary point with a vanishing second derivative
questions.prompt_html:
A curve is defined by

\[x=t+\ln t,\qquad y=t^2-at+b\ln t,\qquad t\gt 0,\]

where \(a,b\) are real constants. At \(t=1\), both \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) are zero.

  1. Find \(a\) and \(b\).

    [4]

  2. For these constants, find and factorise both derivatives in terms of \(t\).

    [4]

  3. Determine the nature of the point with \(t=1\) and give its tangent.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

At \(t=1\), \(x_t=2\). The condition \(y_x=0\) is \(y_t=2-a+b=0\). At a point where \(y_t=0\), the parametric formula gives \(y_{xx}=y_{tt}/x_t^2\). Since \(y_{tt}(1)=2-b\), the second condition gives \(b=2\), and then \(a=4\).

(b)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=1 + \frac{1}{t},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=2 t - 4 + \frac{2}{t}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2 \left(t - 1\right)^{2}}{t + 1}.\]

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=\frac{2 \left(t - 1\right) \left(t + 3\right)}{\left(t + 1\right)^{2}}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{2 t \left(t - 1\right) \left(t + 3\right)}{\left(t + 1\right)^{3}}.\]

(c)

The first derivative is non-negative for all t>0 and positive except at t=1, so there is no local maximum or minimum. The second derivative is negative for 0<t<1 and positive for t>1. Since x_t>0, this is also a change of concavity as x increases. Therefore \((1,-3)\) is a stationary point of inflection. Its tangent is \(y=-3\).

questions.title: An inverse sine of a hyperbolic function
questions.prompt_html:
